Getting startedLanguage examples

Save window values and connect controls to the server

This guide starts with a local tool containing text fields, a slider and a list. You will see how to open two copies without sharing their values. After that, you can add your own drawing and input, or connect a panel to items and fluids stored on the server.

Start with the first section if you are building a normal settings or tools window. The custom-screen section is optional: use it when the supplied controls cannot draw or handle something you need. The server-storage section is for inventory and fluid access. Each section has its own code; you do not need to combine all three to open a window.

Select your language above the code block. The Java snippets are classes you add to your addon; keep local screen code in client-only classes. A callback is a function you give the library to run later, such as when text changes. A controller is the object in your addon that keeps a window handle and closes it when the tool is finished.

Choose where to keep a value

Suppose two windows both contain a name field. Usually, typing in one should not change the other. A value stored in each screen gives you that separation. If several pages in one window need the same name, put it in that window’s WindowState instead. Use the table to choose the lifetime your value needs.

Value lifetime
StoreUse it forHow long it lasts
Screen fields and unbound widgetsText, selection or scroll position used by one pageUntil that screen is removed. A retained parent keeps its values while a child page is shown.
WindowStateA counter or setting that pages in the same window shareUntil that window closes. Another window has a separate store.
Your addon's captured variablesData you deliberately share between windowsAs long as your addon retains it. A callback does not turn an outer variable into a per-window value.
Existing server storagePlayer inventory, machine slots, fluid tanks or saved settingsAccording to the storage owner's rules. Closing the panel ends access through that panel; it does not delete the stored contents.

Window and screen values are held in memory. They are not saved to disk automatically. For settings that must survive a restart, see the settings window walkthrough.

Give each window its own counter and text fields

First, describe the controls you want. Call WidgetSpec.widget(kind, id, x, y, width, height) for each one, choose its options and finish with build(). This produces a description the library can reuse. It does not put a control on screen yet.

In the Java code below, controls() returns these descriptions as a list. The open() method passes that list to WidgetScreen.open(title, width, height, controls) twice: once for Tools A and once for Tools B. Each call creates fresh widgets and returns a handle for its window. The fields first and second keep those handles for closing later.

Choose the control’s type and rectangle using these arguments. Positions and sizes use Minecraft GUI units, so GUI scale can make them differ from desktop pixels.

Control arguments
ArgumentMeaning
kindThe control type, such as TEXT_FIELD, SLIDER, CHECKBOX, LIST or SCROLL.
idA stable ID used to find this control in its screen.
x, yThe control's position in GUI units. A nested control is positioned inside its parent.
width, heightThe control's size in GUI units.

Next, add options to the control description before calling build(). For example, initial("Hello") supplies starting text and maxLength(40) limits what the field accepts. Use only options that belong to that kind of control.

Set the initial value and input rules
CallWhat to passResult
initial(value)A value appropriate for the controlChoose the starting text, slider value, checkbox state or list selection.
maxLength(length)Maximum text lengthLimit text input.
validate(predicate)A function that accepts or rejects textAccept the change only when the function returns true.
range(minimum, maximum, step)Slider limits and step sizeChoose the allowed slider values.
choices(entries)List entriesChoose the values shown by a list.
bind(name)A named entry in the window storeConnect this control to a value that can survive navigation.
changed(callback)A function receiving the live widgetReact to a change on the client thread. Use the widget's state access for that window's data.

The name field also has a changed callback. When its text changes, the library passes the live widget to that function. Calling widget.state() gives the window store belonging to that widget, so the callback updates the right window.

Inside that callback, state.initial("changes", 0) creates the counter if it is missing. If it already exists as an integer, its value is kept. The next line reads it, adds one and writes it back with state.integer("changes", nextValue). This counter is stored in memory; the sample does not draw it as a label. Use a different key if you also want to store text, because one key cannot hold both types.

To use the Java class, keep one WindowWidgetsRecipe object in your client controller and call its open() method from a button or key action. Call it once to create the pair. Calling it again creates another pair rather than bringing the first pair forward, so close the current pair before replacing it. Later, call the same object’s close() method from your client disconnect or tool-close action.

import java.util.List;
import com.sbancuz.offscreen.api.OffscreenAPI;
import com.sbancuz.offscreen.api.widgets.WidgetSpec;
import com.sbancuz.offscreen.api.widgets.WidgetScreen;
import com.sbancuz.offscreen.window.Window;
import static com.sbancuz.offscreen.api.widgets.WidgetSpec.Kind.*;

final class WindowWidgetsRecipe {
    private Window first;
    private Window second;

    // Client initialization: these declarations can be reused for every new window.
    static List<WidgetSpec> controls() {
        var name = WidgetSpec.widget(TEXT_FIELD, "name", 12, 12, 180, 20)
                .initial("Hello").maxLength(40).validate(text -> !text.contains("\n"))
                .changed(widget -> {
                    var state = widget.state();
                    state.initial("changes", 0);
                    state.integer("changes", state.integer("changes") + 1);
                }).build();
        var volume = WidgetSpec.widget(SLIDER, "volume", 12, 40, 180, 20)
                .range(0, 1, 0.05).initial(0.5).build();
        var enabled = WidgetSpec.widget(CHECKBOX, "enabled", 12, 68, 180, 20)
                .label("Enabled").initial(true).build();
        var choice = WidgetSpec.widget(LIST, "choice", 12, 96, 180, 48)
                .choices(List.of("Copper", "Silver", "Gold")).build();
        var nested = WidgetSpec.widget(TEXT_FIELD, "notes", 4, 90, 160, 20).build();
        var scroll = WidgetSpec.widget(SCROLL, "scroll", 220, 12, 180, 80)
                .children(List.of(nested)).build();
        return List.of(name, volume, enabled, choice, scroll);
    }

    // Client action: each call creates new screens and independent WindowState values.
    void open() {
        var declaration = controls();
        first = WidgetScreen.open("Tools A", 640, 400, declaration);
        second = WidgetScreen.open("Tools B", 640, 400, declaration);
    }

    // Client teardown: retaining a widget after its screen closes does not keep it alive.
    void close() {
        OffscreenAPI.close(first);
        OffscreenAPI.close(second);
    }
}

class WindowWidgetsRecipeK {
    private var first: Window? = null
    private var second: Window? = null

    // Client initialization: the shared Java model owns validation and live-instance creation.
    fun controls(): List<WidgetSpec> = listOf(
        widget(TEXT_FIELD, "name", 12, 12, 180, 20) {
            initial("Hello"); maxLength(40); validate {
                !it.contains("\n")
            }
            changed { field ->
                val state = field.state()
                state.initial("changes", 0)
                state.integer("changes", state.integer("changes") + 1)
            }
        },
        widget(SLIDER,
            "volume",
            12,
            40,
            180,
            20) {
            range(0.0,
            1.0,
            0.05); initial(0.5)
        },
        widget(CHECKBOX,
            "enabled",
            12,
            68,
            180,
            20) {
            label("Enabled"); initial(true)
        },
        widget(LIST,
            "choice",
            12,
            96,
            180,
            48) {
            choices(listOf("Copper",
            "Silver",
            "Gold"))
        },
        widget(SCROLL, "scroll", 220, 12, 180, 80) {
            children(listOf(widget(TEXT_FIELD, "notes", 4, 90, 160, 20) {}))
        },
    )

    // Client action: a declaration can be opened twice without sharing its input or selections.
    fun open() {
        val declaration = controls().toTypedArray()
        first = openWidgets("Tools A", 640, 400, *declaration)
        second = openWidgets("Tools B", 640, 400, *declaration)
    }

    // Client teardown; ordinary captured mutable variables are still shared by their closures.
    fun close() {
        OffscreenAPI.close(first);
        OffscreenAPI.close(second)
    }
}

final class WindowWidgetsRecipeS:
  private var first: Window = null
  private var second: Window = null

  // Client initialization; each lambda configures the shared typed Java builder.
  def controls(): Seq[WidgetSpec] = Seq(
    widget(TEXT_FIELD, "name", 12, 12, 180, 20) { field =>
      field.initial("Hello").maxLength(40).validate(text => !text.contains("\n"))
      field.changed { control =>
        val state = control.state()
        state.initial("changes", Int.box(0))
        state.integer("changes", state.integer("changes") + 1)
      }
    },
    widget(SLIDER,
        "volume",
        12,
        40,
        180,
        20)(_.range(0,
        1,
        0.05)
        .initial(Double.box(0.5))),
    widget(CHECKBOX,
        "enabled",
        12,
        68,
        180,
        20)(_.label("Enabled")
        .initial(Boolean.box(true))),
    widget(LIST,
        "choice",
        12,
        96,
        180,
        48)(_.choices(JList.of("Copper",
        "Silver",
        "Gold"))),
    widget(SCROLL, "scroll", 220, 12, 180, 80) { panel =>
      panel.children(JList.of(widget(TEXT_FIELD, "notes", 4, 90, 160, 20)(_ => ())))
    }
  )

  // Client action; native Scala 3 uses Scalar, with no alternate widget implementation.
  def open(): Unit =
    val declaration = controls()
    first = openWidgets("Tools A", 640, 400)(declaration*)
    second = openWidgets("Tools B", 640, 400)(declaration*)

  // Client teardown.
  def close(): Unit =
    OffscreenAPI.close(first)
    OffscreenAPI.close(second)
#side client
import mods.offscreencleanroom.Windows;

// Client initialization: defaults are copied into each newly opened window.
val tools = Windows.screen("Tools", 640, 400);
tools.defaults.integer("changes", 0);
tools.textField("name", 12, 12, 180, 20, "Hello").maxLength(40)
    .validate(function(text) {
        return text != "rejected";
    })
    .changed(function(field) {
        field.state.integer("changes", field.state.integer("changes") + 1);
    });
tools.slider("volume", 12, 40, 180, 20, 0.0, 1.0, 0.05, 0.5);
tools.checkbox("enabled", 12, 68, 180, 20, true).label("Enabled");
tools.list("choice", 12, 96, 180, 48, ["Copper", "Silver", "Gold"]);
val scroll = tools.scrollPanel("scroll", 220, 12, 180, 80);
scroll.add(tools.textField("notes", 4, 90, 160, 20, ""));

// Call from your client input action after Minecraft has initialized its graphics context.
function openTools(tools as mods.offscreencleanroom.Screen) as void {
    val first = tools.open();
    val second = tools.open();
    // Retain both handles in your controller. Its later teardown calls first.close() and second.close().
}

After opening the pair, type a different name in each window and change their controls independently. The text fields in this sample are not bound to named window entries, so their text belongs to their individual screens. Only the change counter uses WindowState.

If you later add another page that needs the same name, use bind("name") to connect its field to that window’s named value. For a change made by your own code, use the live widget’s setter when you want validation and change callbacks to run. Writing a value directly to WindowState only updates the store.

The built-in controls already handle text selection, clipboard shortcuts and keyboard focus. Tab moves forward and Shift+Tab moves backward. You only need the custom callbacks in the next section if your screen needs extra behavior.

Handle drawing and input for a custom screen

You can skip this section if the built-in controls cover your tool. For custom behavior, the library needs to know how to draw your screen, deliver input and clean it up. HostUIBuilder.forScreen(screen) lets you provide those functions. The finished object connects your screen to the window and is called an adapter.

In the Java class below, Scratch holds the text and counters for one screen. The adapter(screen) method attaches functions to that particular object. For example, its text callback adds the entered text to screen.text, and its draw callback displays that field. The functions share the screen object, so drawing sees the latest input.

Choose callbacks according to the work you need to do:

Screen callbacks
CallCallback inputYour code should
draw(callback)Frame informationDraw the current screen. Keep OpenGL and font work inside this client render callback.
resize(callback)New GUI width and heightRecalculate positions and sizes for the available space.
tick(callback)No argumentsUpdate screen data on the client tick, separately from drawing.
text(callback)Entered textHandle text input, including characters that do not correspond to one key press.
key(callback)Key eventHandle shortcuts or key state. The event also exposes the SDL scancode.
pointer(callback)Pointer eventHandle the supplied mouse action.
scope(scope)A state scopeSupply extra state that must be borrowed and restored around callbacks. Use Scope.NOP when none is needed.
dispose(callback)No argumentsRelease resources and listeners created for this screen.

For input callbacks that return a boolean, return true when your code has handled the event. Return false to leave the normal input handling available. These callbacks run on Minecraft's client thread; declaring them does not call them or open a window.

With those functions attached, call build() to finish the adapter. The Java open() method then passes two functions to OffscreenAPI.open: Scratch::new creates a fresh screen, and the second function builds the adapter for it. Offscreen calls both during opening and keeps the result in the returned window.

Keep an AdapterRecipe object in your client controller. Call its open() from client input and its close() during teardown. After installation, the window calls the adapter’s disposal function when that screen is removed. Put screen-owned listeners and graphics cleanup there; in this small sample, disposal only clears the screen’s text.

import com.sbancuz.offscreen.api.HostUI;
import com.sbancuz.offscreen.api.HostUIBuilder;
import com.sbancuz.offscreen.api.OffscreenAPI;
import com.sbancuz.offscreen.scope.Scope;
import com.sbancuz.offscreen.window.Window;
import net.minecraft.client.gui.GuiScreen;

final class AdapterRecipe {
    static final class Scratch extends GuiScreen {
        String text = "Type here";
        int ticks, layoutWidth, lastScancode;
    }
    private Window window;

    // Client initialization: every adapter gets a fresh backing screen and its own fields.
    static HostUI adapter(Scratch screen) {
        return HostUIBuilder.forScreen(screen)
                .draw(frame -> frame.minecraft().fontRenderer.drawString(screen.text,
                    8,
                    24,
                    -1,
                    true))
                .resize((width, height) -> screen.layoutWidth = width)
                .tick(() -> screen.ticks++)
                .text(text -> {
                    screen.text += text; return true;
                })
                .key(key -> {
                    screen.lastScancode = key.sdlScanCode(); return false;
                })
                .pointer(event -> false) // False preserves normal vanilla control handling.
                .scope(Scope.NOP)        // Replace with an addon scope if extra state must be borrowed.
                .dispose(() -> screen.text = "")
                .build();
    }
    // Client action: supplier and adapter creation are immediate; callbacks run on the client thread.
    void open() {
        window = OffscreenAPI.open(Scratch::new,
        value -> adapter((Scratch) value));
    }
    // Client teardown. Both the backing GUI and custom disposal are attempted, even after an exception.
    void close() {
        OffscreenAPI.close(window);
    }
}
import com.sbancuz.offscreen.api.*
import com.sbancuz.offscreen.scope.Scope
import com.sbancuz.offscreen.window.Window
import net.minecraft.client.gui.GuiScreen

class AdapterRecipeK {
    class Scratch : GuiScreen() {
        var text = "Type here"
        var ticks = 0
        var layoutWidth = 0
        var lastScancode = 0
    }
    private var window: Window? = null

    // Client initialization. The Kotlin receiver configures the same HostUIBuilder as Java.
    fun adapter(screen: Scratch): HostUI = hostUI(screen) {
        draw {
            frame -> frame.minecraft().fontRenderer.drawString(screen.text,
            8f,
            24f,
            -1,
            true)
        }
        resize { width, _ -> screen.layoutWidth = width }
        tick { screen.ticks++ }
        text {
            value -> screen.text += value;
            true
        }
        key {
            event -> screen.lastScancode = event.sdlScanCode();
            false
        }
        pointer { false }
        scope(Scope.NOP)
        dispose { screen.text = "" }
    }
    // Client action; screen fields belong to this open, rather than a shared outer script counter.
    fun open() {
        window = openWindow(HostUIFactory {
            value -> adapter(value as Scratch)
        }) {
            Scratch()
        }
    }
    // Client teardown.
    fun close() { OffscreenAPI.close(window) }
}

import com.sbancuz.offscreen.api.{HostUI, HostUIFactory, OffscreenAPI}
import com.sbancuz.offscreen.scaladsl.Offscreen.hostUI
import com.sbancuz.offscreen.scope.Scope
import com.sbancuz.offscreen.window.Window
import net.minecraft.client.gui.GuiScreen

final class AdapterRecipeS:
  final class Scratch extends GuiScreen:
    var text = "Type here"
    var ticks = 0
    var layoutWidth = 0
    var lastScancode = 0
  private var window: Window = null

  // Client initialization, using the same typed callback builder as Java and Kotlin.
  def adapter(screen: Scratch): HostUI = hostUI(screen) { builder =>
    builder.draw(frame => { frame.minecraft().fontRenderer.drawString(screen.text,
        8,
        24,
        -1,
        true); () })
      .resize((width, height) => screen.layoutWidth = width)
      .tick(() => screen.ticks += 1)
      .text(value => { screen.text += value; true })
      .key(event => { screen.lastScancode = event.sdlScanCode(); false })
      .pointer(_ => false)
      .scope(Scope.NOP)
      .dispose(() => screen.text = "")
  }
  // Client action. Native Scala 3 lambdas become the Java callback interfaces.
  def open(): Unit =
    window = OffscreenAPI.open(() => new Scratch(),
        (value: Object) => adapter(value.asInstanceOf[Scratch]))
  // Client teardown.
  def close(): Unit = OffscreenAPI.close(window)
#side client
import mods.offscreencleanroom.Windows;

// Client initialization. Host scopes are supplied automatically by this facade.
val scratch = Windows.screen("Scratch", 640, 400);
scratch.defaults.text("input", "Type here");
scratch.defaults.integer("ticks", 0);
scratch.on("tick", function(event) {
    event.state.integer("ticks", event.state.integer("ticks") + 1);
    return false;
});
scratch.on("text", function(event) {
    event.state.text("input", event.state.text("input") + event.text);
    return true;
});
scratch.on("key", function(event) {
    print(event.scancode); return false;
});
scratch.on("resize", function(event) {
    print(event.width); return false;
});
scratch.on("click", function(event) {
    return false;
});
scratch.on("drag", function(event) {
    return false;
});
scratch.on("release", function(event) {
    return false;
});
scratch.on("scroll", function(event) {
    return false;
});
scratch.on("draw", function(event) {
    // Render callback. The draw/state context expires when this callback returns.
    event.text(event.state.text("input"), 8, 24, -1, true);
    return false;
});
scratch.on("close", function(event) {
    print("Scratch closed"); return false;
});
// Client action after graphics initialization: retain scratch.open(), then close that handle at teardown.
// CraftTweaker 1.12 startup scripts require a restart after editing; this is not a Groovy reload registration.

GroovyScript adapter registrations belong to the script that installed them. Reload removes those registrations and stops their old callbacks. Ordinary CraftTweaker startup scripts take effect after a game restart; their screen-event API uses the same window lifecycle.

Connect item and fluid slots to existing server storage

Local text and counters are enough for a client tool. Items and fluids are different: the server must decide what is stored and whether the player may change it. This section connects a panel to storage your addon already owns.

Before using the code, identify three things in your addon: the item handler, the tank and the access rule for this player. The Java register(inventory, tank, allowed) method receives functions that find or check them. You must supply these functions from your own machine or player-storage code. The sample cannot run as an inventory tool until that storage exists.

First, call SyncedPanel.backend during common initialization to give those functions a name. This named connection is called a backend. The panel uses the name to request storage when a player opens it.

Backend registration arguments
ArgumentWhat to supply
nameA stable ID such as example:machine. Both sides must declare matching backend metadata.
permissionA function that checks whether the player may access this storage.
inventoryA function mapping the player to your existing IItemHandler.
tanksA function mapping the player and tank index to an existing IFluidTank.

In this recipe, the backend name is example:machine. Its item function returns the supplied inventory. Its fluid function accepts tank index 0 and returns the supplied tank; other indices are rejected. Replace the name with your own addon’s name and expand that lookup if your machine has more tanks.

The library calls the storage functions on the server after checking permission. Your allowed function must check the rules that matter for your tool, such as machine ownership or player distance. Return storage belonging to the permitted target rather than creating a new empty handler each time the lookup runs.

With the storage connection named, build the panel itself. SyncedPanel.panel("example_tools", "example", 220, 230) takes a factory name, mod ID and panel size in GUI units. Then declare its text, number and flag values before adding controls that use them. The binding name joins the two: the slider uses count because the number was declared with that ID.

The slots use a different kind of binding. Both refer to example:machine, the backend registered above. The item slot’s index selects an inventory slot; the fluid slot’s index selects a tank. The control ID identifies the on-screen control, while the backend and index choose the stored contents it shows.

Connect a panel to values and storage
CallArgumentsMeaning
text(id, initial, maxLength)Binding ID, starting text and length limitDeclare a text value for this session.
number(id, initial, min, max)Binding ID, starting number and boundsDeclare a bounded numeric value.
flag(id, initial)Binding ID and starting booleanDeclare a true/false value.
control(kind, id, binding, x, y, width, height)Control type, ID, value or action name, and GUI rectangleConnect a widget to the declared value or action.
itemSlot(id, backend, index, x, y)Slot ID, backend name, inventory index and GUI positionExpose that slot from the backend's item handler.
fluidSlot(id, backend, index, x, y)Slot ID, backend name, tank index and GUI positionExpose that tank through the panel's fluid control.
action(name, callback)Action name and function receiving a server contextRun the requested change on the server thread.

The Increment button refers to the action named increment. Its server callback adds one to the session’s count, stopping at 100. The callback receives a temporary context for reading and changing those session values. Use it inside the callback only; saving that context in a field does not keep it valid.

Finally, register() returns an OffscreenSimpleFactory. Store it during common initialization on both sides. After joining a world, call that factory’s openOffscreen() from client input and keep the returned window. For the full opening and closing sequence, follow ModularUI and HEI.

import java.util.function.Function;
import java.util.function.Predicate;
import com.sbancuz.offscreen.integration.mui2.SyncedPanel;
import com.sbancuz.offscreen.integration.mui2.OffscreenSimpleFactory;
import net.minecraft.entity.player.EntityPlayer;
import net.minecraftforge.items.IItemHandler;
import net.minecraftforge.fluids.IFluidTank;

final class SyncedPanelRecipe {
    // Common initialization, once on both sides. These functions resolve existing addon storage.
    // Offscreen calls them only on the server, after the permission predicate succeeds.
    static OffscreenSimpleFactory register(Function<EntityPlayer,
        IItemHandler> inventory,
            Function<EntityPlayer, IFluidTank> tank, Predicate<EntityPlayer> allowed) {
        SyncedPanel.backend("example:machine", allowed, inventory, (player, index) -> {
            if (index != 0) throw new IllegalArgumentException("Only tank 0 exists");
            return tank.apply(player);
        });
        return SyncedPanel.panel("example_tools", "example", 220, 230)
                .permission(allowed)
                .text("name", "", 32).number("count", 0, 0, 100).flag("enabled", false)
                // Server action: the borrowed context expires even if this callback throws.
                .action("increment",
                    context -> context.number("count",
                    Math.min(100,
                    context.number("count") + 1)))
                .control("button", "Increment", "increment", 10, 10, 90, 20)
                .control("text", "Name", "name", 10, 40, 140, 20)
                .control("slider", "Count", "count", 10, 70, 140, 20)
                .control("checkbox", "Enabled", "enabled", 10, 100, 90, 20)
                .itemSlot("input", "example:machine", 0, 170, 40)
                .fluidSlot("tank", "example:machine", 0, 170, 70)
                .playerInventory(10, 140).register();
    }
    // Client action, after joining a world: factory.openOffscreen().
    // Retain its window; client teardown uses OffscreenAPI.close(window).
}

    // Common initialization, once on both sides. Only the server invokes these storage resolvers.
    fun register(inventory: Function<EntityPlayer,
        IItemHandler>,
        tank: Function<EntityPlayer,
        IFluidTank>,
                 allowed: Predicate<EntityPlayer>): OffscreenSimpleFactory {
        SyncedPanel.backend("example:machine", allowed, inventory) { player, index ->
            require(index == 0) { "Only tank 0 exists" }
            tank.apply(player)
        }
        return SyncedPanel.panel("example_tools",
            "example",
            220,
            230)
            .permission(allowed)
            .text("name",
                "",
                32)
            .number("count",
                0.0,
                0.0,
                100.0)
            .flag("enabled",
                false)
            // Server action. The context belongs only to this callback and this container.
            .action("increment") {
                context -> context.number("count",
                minOf(100.0,
                context.number("count") + 1))
            }
            .control("button", "Increment", "increment", 10, 10, 90, 20)
            .control("text", "Name", "name", 10, 40, 140, 20)
            .control("slider", "Count", "count", 10, 70, 140, 20)
            .control("checkbox", "Enabled", "enabled", 10, 100, 90, 20)
            .itemSlot("input", "example:machine", 0, 170, 40)
            .fluidSlot("tank", "example:machine", 0, 170, 70)
            .playerInventory(10, 140).register()
    }
    // Client action: factory.openOffscreen(); retain the window until client teardown.
}

import java.util.function.{Function, Predicate}
import com.sbancuz.offscreen.integration.mui2.{SyncedPanel, OffscreenSimpleFactory}
import net.minecraft.entity.player.EntityPlayer
import net.minecraftforge.items.IItemHandler
import net.minecraftforge.fluids.IFluidTank

object SyncedPanelRecipeS:
  // Common initialization, once on both sides. Resolvers run only on the authorized server.
  def register(inventory: Function[EntityPlayer,
      IItemHandler],
      tank: Function[EntityPlayer,
      IFluidTank],
               allowed: Predicate[EntityPlayer]): OffscreenSimpleFactory =
    SyncedPanel.backend("example:machine", allowed, inventory, (player, index) =>
      require(index == 0, "Only tank 0 exists")
      tank.apply(player)
    )
    SyncedPanel.panel("example_tools", "example", 220, 230).permission(allowed)
      .text("name", "", 32).number("count", 0, 0, 100).flag("enabled", false)
      // Server action: context access ends when this callback returns.
      .action("increment",
          context => context.number("count",
          math.min(100,
          context.number("count") + 1)))
      .control("button", "Increment", "increment", 10, 10, 90, 20)
      .control("text", "Name", "name", 10, 40, 140, 20)
      .control("slider", "Count", "count", 10, 70, 140, 20)
      .control("checkbox", "Enabled", "enabled", 10, 100, 90, 20)
      .itemSlot("input", "example:machine", 0, 170, 40)
      .fluidSlot("tank", "example:machine", 0, 170, 70)
      .playerInventory(10, 140).register()
  // Client action: factory.openOffscreen(); close the retained window during client teardown.
import mods.offscreencleanroom.Windows;

// Common startup, identical on client and server. An addon must register example:machine first.
// Its server resolver and permission check choose the actual inventory/tank; scripts pass only the name.
val panel = Windows.panel("example_tools", "example", 220, 230)
    .text("name", "", 32).number("count", 0.0, 0.0, 100.0).flag("enabled", false)
    .action("increment", function(context) {
        // Server action. The upper bound is also checked on incoming slider changes.
        val next = context.number("count") + 1.0;
        if (next <= 100.0) context.number("count", next);
    })
    .control("button", "Increment", "increment", 10, 10, 90, 20)
    .control("text", "Name", "name", 10, 40, 140, 20)
    .control("slider", "Count", "count", 10, 70, 140, 20)
    .control("checkbox", "Enabled", "enabled", 10, 100, 90, 20)
    .itemSlot("input", "example:machine", 0, 170, 40)
    .fluidSlot("tank", "example:machine", 0, 170, 70)
    .playerInventory(10, 140);
val factoryName = panel.register();

// A client input action may call Windows.openSynchronized(factoryName).
// Retain its window and call close() from the controller's later client teardown.

CraftTweaker refers to a registered backend by name instead of passing Java handler objects. A mismatch between the two sides rejects the open before storage is resolved. This follows Minecraft's one-active-container rule; opening another desktop window does not provide another independent server inventory.

Panel text, numbers and flags last for the session. The item handler and tanks still belong to your addon. Closing the window releases the panel connection; your addon remains responsible for saving its storage and releasing resources it created outside the panel.

Handle reloads, errors, and cleanup

Once your tool is working, connect its close method to your addon’s client disconnect or unload hook. For the local recipes, that method closes the handles saved in their fields. For the server panel, close the window returned by the factory. Releasing a widget or panel does not close unrelated files, workers or listeners your addon kept elsewhere, so give those resources their own cleanup code.

The table below explains what happens when navigation, reloading or failure changes the screen’s lifetime. Use it to decide which references your controller can still use.

What is kept or removed after each action
WhenOutcome
Another window opensIt receives new defaults and independent live widgets.
A parent screen returnsIts existing instance and the window’s values are retained; resize requests relayout.
Scripts reloadOwned callbacks expire first. Exact adapter receipts and owned windows are then released.
A callback throwsBorrowed contexts expire in finally. A failing local window or server callback closes its own session; other owned cleanup still runs.
A session closes or loses permissionStale actions and slot interactions are rejected; backend permission is checked again before synchronization.

Tell an open window from a ready screen

One final step matters when you open the server panel: the returned window may appear before its contents are ready. It can show a waiting message or an error while still being open. Keep its handle and check its status from a later client tick.

Use isOpen when deciding whether the window still exists. Use isReady before code that needs the installed screen’s layout. To show progress or explain a failure, read getStatus and report its message when the status changes. The code below demonstrates that check; call report(window) with the handle you saved from opening.

Return from your input handler rather than waiting for readiness in a loop. Minecraft needs its client thread free to receive the server reply and finish layout.

Window status calls
CallWhat it tells you
isOpen(window)Whether the native window still exists.
isReady(window)Whether screen layout has completed and synchronized bindings are healthy.
getStatus(window)A status snapshot with a state and message, useful when reporting a change or failure.
close(window)End this window's session and release its resources when your controller finishes.

Java, Kotlin, Scala and Groovy read the same status snapshot. The ZenScript handle exposes open, ready, status, failureReason and statusMessage. Empty failure strings mean no failure. On the local error screen, Retry starts a fresh request and Close ends the attempt; a late reply from the previous request cannot make it ready.

import com.sbancuz.offscreen.api.OffscreenAPI;
import com.sbancuz.offscreen.window.Window;

final class ReadinessExample {
    // Client initialization: retain the Window returned by your factory.
    // Client action/tick: call on a status change; do not block waiting for readiness.
    static void report(Window window) {
        var status = OffscreenAPI.getStatus(window);
        System.out.println(status.state() + ": " + status.message());
        if (!OffscreenAPI.isReady(window)) return;
        // The screen has completed layout; synchronized bindings are healthy.
        System.out.println("Screen is ready");
    }
    // Teardown: OffscreenAPI.close(window). The error screen also offers Close/Retry.
}
import com.sbancuz.offscreen.api.OffscreenAPI
import com.sbancuz.offscreen.window.Window

// Client action/tick: inspect a retained handle on status changes, without blocking.
fun reportReadiness(window: Window?) {
    val status = OffscreenAPI.getStatus(window)
    println("${status.state()}: ${status.message()}")
    if (!OffscreenAPI.isReady(window)) return
    println("Screen is ready")
}
// Client teardown: OffscreenAPI.close(window). Close/Retry are also in the error screen.

// Client teardown/reload: OffscreenAPI.close(window). A factory handle is controller-owned.
import com.sbancuz.offscreen.api.OffscreenAPI
import com.sbancuz.offscreen.window.Window

// Client action/tick: inspect the retained handle on status changes; never block.
def reportReadiness(window: Window): Unit =
    val status = OffscreenAPI.getStatus(window)
    println(s"${status.state()}: ${status.message()}")
    if OffscreenAPI.isReady(window) then println("Screen is ready")
// Client teardown: OffscreenAPI.close(window). The error screen also has Close/Retry.
#side client
import mods.offscreencleanroom.Window;

// Client action: pass the handle returned by Windows.openSynchronized or your panel.
// Call on status changes, not every frame. Do not run rendering helpers on the server.
function reportReadiness(window as Window) {
    print(window.status + ": " + window.statusMessage);
    if (window.failureReason != "") print(window.failureReason);
    if (!window.ready) return;
    print("Screen is ready");
}
// Teardown: window.close(). The local error screen also provides Close and Retry.
